data.title: US inflation keeps pressure on the Fed as Nvidia’s selloff spreads
data.description:
Referenced assets

  • US headline CPI rose 0.4% in October, down from 0.6% in September but above the 0.3% consensus.
  • Core CPI rose 0.3% for a third consecutive month, pointing to persistent inflation beyond energy.
  • A 25-basis-point Fed hike in December remains the base case. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a 50-basis-point move could warrant discussion if core inflation stays elevated.
  • Nvidia shares were down nearly 27% since the start of November following Jensen Huang’s removal as CEO.
  • The selloff spread to chipmakers, data center operators and energy companies as investors reassessed the pace of AI infrastructure spending.

Slower energy inflation brings down headline CPI

US consumer prices rose 0.4% month on month in October, slowing from 0.6% in September. The reading still exceeded the 0.3% consensus. Energy accounted for most of the slowdown, with prices rising 0.7% after a 5.2% jump in September. Food prices rose 0.5% after holding steady the previous month, while shelter inflation eased to 0.3% from 0.4%.

Core CPI rose 0.3% for a third straight month, indicating that price pressures persisted beyond the energy shock. As expected, the Bureau of Labor Statistics did not publish year-on-year rates because the previous year’s government shutdown disrupted data collection. At an annualized pace, the recent monthly core CPI readings remain well above the 2% rate the Fed targets for PCE inflation.

Waller backs a quarter-point hike but leaves room for a larger move

Fed Governor Christopher Waller backed a 25-basis-point rate increase in December. He said a larger move of 50 basis points would warrant consideration if monthly core CPI inflation remained at around 0.3% or higher.

Waller described the US economy as strong and the labor market as stable. He also said inflation remained too high and monetary policy was less restrictive than he had previously thought. In his view, too small a hike amid persistent inflation could undermine the Fed’s credibility. He also stressed the need to avoid cooling the economy excessively. A quarter-point hike remains the base case for December.

Nvidia’s selloff hits companies tied to AI spending

Nvidia’s board removed co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang following reports about his private life. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress took over as interim CEO, and the company began searching for a permanent successor. After the sharp selloff, Nvidia shares were down nearly 27% since the start of November.

Losses spread to semiconductor manufacturers, data center operators and energy companies. The leadership change at a key chip supplier prompted investors to reassess how quickly AI infrastructure projects would move ahead. Delays could push back orders for chips and servers and temper expectations for growth in electricity demand. Those expectations had supported valuations well beyond the technology sector. At the same time, the prospect of higher US interest rates put additional pressure on companies whose valuations depend heavily on earnings expected several years from now.

data.title: Nvidia (NVDA) Q3 earnings preview: AI spending risks and governance concerns threaten major uptrend
data.description:
Referenced assets

Key Takeaways

  • Nvidia faces high earnings expectations: Q3 revenue and EPS are forecast to rise around 90% year-on-year, putting AI demand and profitability under scrutiny.
  • AI financing and governance risks mount: Q4 guidance is crucial as investors assess hyperscaler capex sustainability and reported allegations involving CEO Jensen Huang.
  • NVDA bearish below 201.66: A break below 152.90 could expose 129.16, while a daily close above 201.66 would invalidate the bearish outlook.

Ahead of next Tuesday’s Q3 FY2027 earnings, Nvidia (NVDA) faces a critical test of investor confidence as concerns over the sustainability of the AI infrastructure spending boom are now compounded by an emerging corporate governance controversy involving CEO Jensen Huang.

Nvidia’s shares fell 4.3% on Monday, 9 November 2026, wiping approximately US$190 billion off its market capitalisation, following reports of an investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by an alleged Chinese intelligence operation.

The development has added a new layer of uncertainty to the company’s leadership, US-China regulatory exposure and elevated valuation.

Overall, the most valuable company in the world is now facing a double whammy of macro and micro headwinds that led to a significant decline of almost 30% in Nvidia’s market capitalisation in a span of less than one month, from a peak of US$5.77 trillion on 6 October 2026 to US$4.07 trillion on Tuesday, 10 November 2026.

The AI juggernaut is scheduled to release its results at approximately 4:20 pm US Eastern Time on Tuesday, 17 November 2026, followed by its earnings conference call at 5 pm ET (6 am Singapore time on Wednesday, 18 November 2026).

Based on the street’s consensus, revenue and earnings growth are expected to be rosy: revenue is expected to increase a whopping 90.9% year-on-year to US$108.84 billion, while EPS is expected to skyrocket 90% year-on-year to US$2.47.

Ahead of Nvidia’s Q3 FY2027 earnings release, options markets are pricing an approximately ±10.6% move in Nvidia’s shares (NVDA) as of 10 November 2026, above its 10-year average peak earnings-day movement of ±7.8%, according to data from EarningsWatcher.

Why Nvidia’s earnings matter to the broader US stock market: circular financing raises contagion risks across the AI ecosystem

Nvidia’s upcoming earnings could have significant implications for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100, given its substantial index weighting and increasingly interconnected financial relationships across the US artificial intelligence ecosystem.

Nvidia accounted for approximately 8.18% of the Nasdaq 100 as of 20 October 2026, meaning a 5% movement in its shares alone could move the index by roughly 0.41 percentage points, assuming other constituents remain unchanged.

More importantly, growing concerns over circular financing, where Nvidia invests in, provides financing support to, or guarantees obligations involving AI infrastructure companies that subsequently purchase its chips, have raised questions about the independence and sustainability of AI-related demand.

In August, Nvidia announced a financing initiative targeting more than US$500 billion in third-party capital, with potential company-backed guarantees of up to US$125 billion.

These arrangements could amplify contagion risks: a slowdown in AI demand or tightening credit conditions could weaken data-centre operators’ cash flows, restrict their ability to finance new chip purchases and ultimately weigh on Nvidia’s future revenue growth.

Such a development could trigger simultaneous selling across semiconductor manufacturers, hyperscalers, AI infrastructure providers and private-credit-exposed financial institutions.

Consequently, a stronger-than-expected Nvidia earnings beat, and robust forward guidance could restore confidence in the broader AI investment cycle, while disappointing results or signs of weakening end-user demand could accelerate the recent sell-off in the Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500.

Let’s now focus on the six key fundamental factors traders should monitor.

1. Data Centre revenue: the principal earnings growth driver

Nvidia’s Data Centre division remains the dominant earnings engine, supported by massive AI infrastructure investment from hyperscalers, cloud service providers and sovereign AI projects.

In Q2 FY2027, Data Centre revenue surged 117% year on year to US$89.0 billion, accounting for approximately 92.5% of total revenue. Overall Q2 revenue reached US$96.2 billion, up 106% year on year.

For Q3, management previously guided to total revenue of US$108 billion, plus or minus 2%, while consensus expectations have risen to approximately US$108.8 billion.

The critical issue is whether the company can continue delivering substantial sequential growth as its revenue base expands.

2. Blackwell and Vera Rubin: Can Nvidia maintain its technological advantage?

Nvidia’s ability to maintain its dominant position in AI accelerators depends heavily on the successful deployment of its Blackwell architecture and next-generation Vera Rubin platform.

In its Q2 results, management confirmed that Vera Rubin had entered full production, with deployments progressing across major cloud partners including Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and CoreWeave.

Traders will focus on production capacity, customer deployment schedules, advanced packaging, and the availability of high-bandwidth memory, alongside competition from AMD and hyperscalers’ internally developed AI chips.

3. Gross margins: a critical test of pricing power

Nvidia’s Q2 non-GAAP gross margin remained at 75%, reflecting its exceptional pricing power within the AI accelerator market.

However, management guided Q3 gross margin lower to 74%, plus or minus 50 basis points, as higher manufacturing, packaging and memory costs potentially weigh on profitability.

With quarterly revenue expected to exceed US$108 billion, even a relatively small change in gross margin can translate into a substantial difference in operating profit.

Traders will assess whether Nvidia can offset rising infrastructure component costs through higher selling prices, product mix and manufacturing efficiencies.

4. Forward guidance: the biggest fundamental catalyst

Nvidia’s earnings reaction will likely depend more on its Q4 FY2027 revenue outlook than its reported Q3 performance.

The market will be looking for confirmation that AI infrastructure orders remain resilient into early 2027, particularly after recent concerns over hyperscaler capital expenditure, AI financing arrangements and the profitability of large-scale AI deployments.

Nvidia has also announced partnerships involving Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR intended to mobilise substantial third-party capital for AI infrastructure development, subject to definitive agreements.8

While these arrangements could broaden financing capacity, investors will scrutinise whether AI infrastructure spending is supported by sustainable end-user demand and cash generation.

5. China export controls and geopolitical risks

China remains both a substantial potential market and a major source of regulatory uncertainty for Nvidia.

Importantly, its Q3 revenue guidance assumes no Data Centre compute revenue from China, reflecting existing restrictions and uncertainties surrounding advanced AI chip exports.

Traders will focus on whether Nvidia can improve its access to Chinese customers, obtain additional export approvals or face tighter restrictions.

This factor is particularly important, given that Nvidia’s proprietary CUDA software ecosystem and its position in the global AI accelerator market depend in part on the breadth of its international customer base.

6. Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with suspected Chinese intelligence operative: a new governance and national security risk

This is the most significant new non-earnings catalyst heading into Nvidia’s Q3 announcement.

According to Reuters reports published on 8–9 November, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after allegations that Jensen Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom US intelligence officials reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.

From an equity valuation perspective, the greater concern is that the investigation could create a prolonged governance discount, especially if it introduces uncertainty over leadership continuity, US export approvals or regulatory compliance.

More importantly, the development coincides with a period of heightened investor scepticism towards the broader AI trade, amplifying the risk of a negative reaction to any earnings disappointment.

Also, any evidence of a security breach, regulatory enforcement action, leadership disruption or additional material disclosures could trigger a sustained valuation derating, even if the company delivers strong earnings.

Fundamental bottom line: What matters most for traders

Nvidia’s Q3 earnings reaction will likely hinge on five key factors: Data Centre revenue growth, Blackwell/Rubin execution, gross margin resilience, Q4 guidance and the implications of the Jensen Huang investigation, with the sustainability of hyperscaler AI spending remaining the overarching fundamental driver.

The bull case is clean earnings beat, accelerating AI infrastructure demand, stronger-than-expected Q4 guidance and resilient gross margins, accompanied by reassuring developments on the corporate governance investigation.

This combination could trigger a sharp recovery in Nvidia’s shares and potentially restore confidence across the wider semiconductor and AI-related technology sectors.

The bear case is not necessarily disappointing headline earnings, but evidence that AI infrastructure spending is losing momentum or that higher costs are beginning to erode profitability.

More importantly, any material escalation in the investigation, particularly involving regulatory enforcement, confirmed security breaches or leadership disruption, could introduce a prolonged governance discount even if Nvidia’s underlying earnings remain strong.

Here’s the charting corner as we dissect NVDA’s multi-week and multi-month outlook from a technical analysis perspective.

Technical analysis: Transitioned into a potential major downtrend phase

The price action of NVDA has staged a bearish breakdown on 30 October 2026 from the 200-day moving average and the “Ascending Wedge” support, following the formation of a major bearish reversal “Ascending Wedge” configuration from the 7 April 2025 low of 86.60 to the current all-time high of 243.37 printed on 6 October 2026 (see Fig. 1).

In addition, the Chaikin Money Flow indicator, a combination of price and volume momentum, has continued to exhibit a bearish momentum condition below the zero centreline.

The volatility-adjusted relative strength (VARS) of NVDA, measured against the broader S&P 500 exchange-traded fund (SPY), continues to show NVDA’s underperformance.

All in all, these observations suggest that NVDA is in a potential major downtrend phase below the 201.66 key medium-term pivotal resistance (also the 200-day moving average).

A break below 152.90, the intermediate support, exposes the medium-term support at 129.16 (also the long-term secular ascending trendline running from the 13 October 2022 low) in the first step.

On the flip side, a clearance and a daily close above 201.66 would invalidate the bearish scenario, opening the door to a potential recovery towards the medium-term resistance at 220.00 (also the 50-day moving average).

data.title: Wall Street under pressure: AI concerns and a strong labor market complicate the outlook
data.description:
Referenced assets

  • Wall Street suffered a sharp sell-off: The S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.5%, as concerns about AI infrastructure investment hit technology stocks.
  • Strong employment data complicated the Fed outlook: U.S. payrolls rose by 165,000 and unemployment fell to 4.1%, giving the Fed more room to keep monetary policy restrictive.
  • Living costs remained a major concern: Despite improving consumer sentiment, 57% of respondents said high prices had reduced their standard of living, while rising oil prices threatened to prolong inflationary pressure.

A sharp sell-off in technology stocks highlighted how heavily Wall Street valuations depend on expectations for the development of artificial intelligence. Concerns about the future of data center investment coincided with disappointing corporate updates. Strong U.S. labor market data released afterward further complicated the monetary policy outlook, while improving consumer sentiment failed to dispel concerns about the high cost of living.

Concerns over AI investment hit Wall Street

The November 5 trading session brought steep declines in U.S. stock indexes. The S&P 500 fell 4.4%, the Dow Jones dropped 3.4%, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 5.5%. The Nasdaq-100 declined even more sharply, falling 6.4%. Semiconductor manufacturers faced the greatest pressure, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index tumbling approximately 12.2%. Although technology companies were at the center of the sell-off, losses spread across all 11 S&P 500 sectors.

One of the main catalysts was a shift in expectations for the expansion of AI infrastructure following the U.S. elections. Victories by Democrats and candidates opposing data center expansion, including in Texas and Georgia, heightened concerns about regulatory restrictions and investment delays. Investors were responding to the risk of future policy decisions. Slower data center construction could delay orders for chips, servers, and energy infrastructure, weakening suppliers’ expected revenue growth.

High valuations amplified the disappointment

The prospect of slower investment challenged the assumptions underpinning the high valuations of AI-related companies. When investors simultaneously lower their earnings forecasts and the price they are willing to pay for future earnings, share prices can react particularly sharply. The scale of the strain was evident in infrastructure suppliers’ stocks. SanDisk shares plunged 22%, AMD, Micron, and Western Digital fell more than 17%. Nvidia dropped approximately 9%.

Corporate earnings and outlook updates also weighed on sentiment. Qualcomm disappointed investors with its smartphone chip sales, and its shares fell approximately 9.5%. Weakness in this segment does not necessarily indicate the state of demand for AI solutions, but it added to caution across the semiconductor industry. Funds reducing their positions and leverage may have intensified the sell-off.

A strong labor market changed the context for the Fed

Another significant development was the October employment report. Nonfarm payrolls increased by 165,000, exceeding economists’ expectations, while the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%. Revisions to the August and September figures also raised earlier estimates by a combined 84,000. Professional and business services recorded the largest employment gain, adding 70,000 jobs. Employment rose by 42,000 in health care, 25,000 in transportation and warehousing, and 19,000 in manufacturing. Private-sector employment posted its strongest increase since March.

These figures highlight the difference between the economy’s current condition and stock market expectations. Technology investment continues to support economic activity and demand for workers, while equity markets are already pricing in the risk that its future growth will slow.

Job growth does not eliminate all signs of weakness

The labor market picture nevertheless remains uneven. The number of people working part time for economic reasons increased by 339,000 to 4.8 million. Meanwhile, the median duration of unemployment rose to 11.9 weeks, its highest level since 2021. Rising employment therefore coexists with difficulties faced by some Americans in finding suitable work. Wage data also sent mixed signals. Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% month over month to $38, exceeding expectations. At the same time, annual wage growth stood at 3.1%, remaining among the lowest rates recorded since 2021.

Stronger employment data give the Federal Reserve more room to maintain restrictive monetary policy. It is worth distinguishing between market reactions on successive days. During Thursday’s stock sell-off, U.S. 10-year Treasury yields fell by approximately 6 basis points, consistent with a shift away from risk. Yields on two-year Treasuries, which are more sensitive to expectations for Fed interest rates, rose only after the employment report was released.

Consumers feel an improvement, but prices still weigh

The preliminary November reading of the University of Michigan survey showed an approximately 6% increase in its consumer sentiment index. Expectations for household finances and business conditions improved. At the same time, sentiment among those with the largest stock portfolios deteriorated by 5%, a decline linked to stock market volatility.

The cost of living remains the main concern. As many as 57% of respondents spontaneously reported that high prices had reduced their standard of living, compared with 46% in February. Despite November’s rebound, overall sentiment was 10% lower than in February, before the conflict with Iran began. A positive signal came from the decline in one-year inflation expectations from 4.7% to 4.3% and in long-term expectations from 3.5% to 3.4%. Both measures, however, remained elevated relative to the earlier levels cited in the survey.

Markets between economic resilience and valuation uncertainty

An additional burden for investors was an approximately 3.9% rise in Brent crude prices to $98.29 a barrel, amid continued uncertainty surrounding the war with Iran. Higher energy prices could make it harder to curb price pressures, even as consumers’ inflation expectations gradually decline.

The U.S. economy continues to show resilience, but strong data are not necessarily unambiguously good news for the stock market. Stable employment supports incomes and consumption while reducing pressure to ease monetary policy. Under these conditions, sustaining high technology stock valuations requires evidence that AI investment will deliver the expected earnings growth. November’s sell-off demonstrated how sharply markets can react when confidence in that scenario begins to weaken.

data.title: Democrats Take Congress, Putting Trump’s Fiscal Agenda to the Test
data.description:
Referenced assets

The midterm result makes further fiscal expansion harder to pass and gives Democrats more leverage over spending and appointments. For markets, the conflict with Iran could still matter more than the shift in Congress.

  • Democrats secured majorities in both chambers, with 243 House seats and 54 Senate seats already projected while counting continued.
  • Further Republican tax cuts and major spending initiatives face a tougher path. Democrats will also need bipartisan support for much of their own legislative agenda.
  • Control of federal spending gives Democrats leverage over the administration’s priorities, including funding for military operations against Iran. A budget standoff could lead to a partial government shutdown.
  • A Democratic Senate can block key presidential nominees, including candidates for the Federal Reserve Board, senior federal posts and the federal courts.
  • A smaller fiscal boost could lower Treasury yields and weigh on the dollar. Renewed escalation with Iran could lift oil prices, delay Fed easing and push the dollar in the opposite direction.

Democrats gain leverage, but major legislation will require compromise

The Democrats’ victory in both chambers exceeded polling expectations and changes the balance of power for the final two years of Donald Trump’s term. The new majority can set the congressional agenda, chair committees and launch investigations into the administration. It also makes it harder for the White House to secure further tax cuts or push through changes to federal benefit programmes.

The legislative constraints run both ways. Most bills still face a 60-vote threshold to end debate in the Senate, and overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in each chamber. Democrats can use popular proposals, such as measures to expand access to healthcare, to put political pressure on the White House. Turning those proposals into law will generally require compromise.

Federal funding offers the clearest test of the new Congress

Control of appropriations gives Democrats a direct way to influence the administration’s priorities. They can press for changes to federal spending and challenge requests for additional funding for military operations against Iran. If Congress and the White House fail to agree on a funding bill, the result could be a partial government shutdown. That gives both sides an incentive to negotiate, even as disagreements over military spending make a deal harder to reach.

Over a longer horizon, the election makes another round of fiscal stimulus less likely. That could moderate growth while easing investor concerns about federal borrowing. The effect may be most visible at the long end of the Treasury curve, where a less expansionary fiscal outlook could reduce the premium investors demand to hold longer-dated debt.

The Senate can constrain appointments while Trump retains room abroad

A Democratic Senate can block or delay nominees to the Federal Reserve Board, the federal courts and senior government posts. That gives Democrats a direct say in who fills future vacancies and makes it harder for Trump to reshape the Fed’s leadership. The outlook for interest rates will still depend primarily on inflation, employment and growth.

With fewer opportunities to advance his domestic agenda through Congress, Trump may turn more often to executive action and foreign policy. Democrats could seek to narrow the president’s tariff powers through legislation, though such a bill would face a potential veto. Congress also has more leverage over the financing of military operations than over the White House’s immediate decisions abroad. Renewed US and Israeli strikes on Iran remain possible, as does a tougher US stance towards Ukraine alongside an effort to improve relations with Russia.

Oil prices could outweigh the fiscal effect on the dollar

A smaller fiscal boost could weigh on the dollar if investors respond by pricing in slower US growth and a more accommodative Fed. For Treasuries, the prospect of less fiscal expansion could reinforce the downward pressure on yields. The durability of that move, however, depends in part on energy prices.

Renewed escalation with Iran could drive oil prices higher, lift inflation expectations and push back the expected timing of Fed rate cuts. That would favour the dollar, particularly if investors also seek safety. The effect on Treasuries would be less clear, as demand for safe assets could offset some of the upward pressure on yields from higher inflation. De-escalation would ease that inflation pressure and give the Fed more room to cut if growth or employment weakens.

Fed independence could gain a stronger safeguard

The election result also offers a potential source of support for the US dollar. A Democratic majority in the Senate makes it harder for President Trump to shape the Federal Reserve’s leadership. If a seat on the Board of Governors becomes vacant, his nominee would need confirmation from a Senate controlled by the opposition.

That limits the scope for politically driven appointments and could strengthen confidence in the Fed’s ability to set monetary policy independently. This could lend support to the dollar over time, even if markets initially focus on the prospect of lower Treasury yields and slower US grow.

Market reaction after the midterms

The US dollar has weakened since the election, while gold has gained and crude oil has sold off sharply. European equities have risen, and Wall Street has reversed its initial decline. Major US indices are now trading above their pre-election levels. The rebound in equities alongside gains in gold suggests investors are weighing different factors across markets, including the outlook for US interest rates and the risk of renewed escalation with Iran.

data.title: XAU/USD Technical & Macro Outlook: October 2026
data.description:
Referenced assets

  • Hawkish Central Bank Expectations: Persistent inflationary pressures (with U.S. CPI at 3.7% in September) keep central banks hawkish, with market pricing leaning toward further Fed rate hikes or a “higher for longer” policy through early 2027.
  • Opposing Macro Forces on Gold: While high inflation provides safe-haven demand for gold, rising Treasury yields and a strong U.S. dollar from central bank tightening increase the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion, creating downside pressure on gold.
  • Technical Bullish Flag Formation: Despite the recent price retreat from peaks near 5,600 within a descending channel, the technical structure views the move as a potential bullish flag pattern within the long-term uptrend since 2023, supported by key support between 4,000–4,120.

Macroeconomic Drivers & Central Bank Policy

Major central banks and economic bureaus are set to publish crucial inflation metrics in late October and early November 2026, including the European Central Bank and Bank of Japan monetary policy meetings on October 29–30, followed by the U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) release for October on November 10. Recent indicators show persistent inflationary pressure driven by sticky energy and shelter costs, with headline U.S. CPI rising to 3.7% year-over-year in September. These upcoming releases will reveal whether price pressures are structural or temporary, determining whether global headline inflation continues to hover well above the target 2% threshold in major economies.

In response, central banks—most notably the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC)—are maintaining a hawkish posture to rein in persistent inflation. Following a 25-basis-point rate hike to a target range of 3.75%–4.00% in September 2026, the FOMC enters its October 27–28 policy meeting under close market scrutiny as officials weigh additional tightening before year-end. If inflation data remain elevated, central banks will keep benchmark rates “higher for longer” or implement incremental rate hikes, thereby dampening economic expansion and cooling consumer demand.

These macroeconomic dynamics exert two opposing forces on gold prices. Higher inflation data initially boosts demand for gold as a traditional inflation hedge and safe-haven store of value. However, persistent inflation triggers hawkish rate responses from the FOMC, driving up real yields on U.S. Treasuries and strengthening the U.S. dollar, thereby increasing the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion and pressuring prices downward. Ultimately, if upcoming CPI prints come in hotter than expected and prompt additional Fed rate hikes, gold is likely to experience short-term selling pressure; conversely, softer inflation data that signals an end to central bank tightening would provide strong tailwinds for a gold rally.

CME FedWatch Rate Expectations

According to CME FedWatch Tool pricing as of October 19, 2026, market expectations are overwhelmingly centered on additional Federal Reserve tightening through early 2027. For the upcoming October 28, 2026 meeting, markets reflect an 82.8% probability that the target rate will settle in the 375–400 bps range (indicating a hold at current levels) and a 17.2% chance of a hike to 400–425 bps. Heading into the final meeting of the year on December 9, 2026, sentiment shifts strongly toward a rate increase, with a 76.5% probability priced for a target range of 400–425 bps and a 15.5% probability placed on a further hike to 425–450 bps.

Looking ahead to the first policy meeting of 2027 on January 27, the market expects rates to remain elevated, with probabilities favoring either maintaining the 400–425 bps target (46.6%) or adjusting upward to the 425–450 bps band (42.1%).

XAU/USD weekly chart technical analysis and COT report updates

  • The price has been moving down within a well-defined descending channel (red trendlines) following a major peak near 5,600. So far, until proven otherwise, the descending channel can be considered a bullish flag formation for the initial long-term uptrend that began in early 2023 and is marked by the blue line.
  • Immediate support lies below price action, between the monthly S1 and the 2023 uptrend, in the 4000-4120 range. A second level of support falls at the annual pivot point of 3829.12.
  • An immediate confluence of resistance lies above price action, at the intersection of the fast EMA9 and the monthly pivot point of 4259.64. A second level of resistance falls near the monthly R1 of 4408.42, intersecting with the upper border of the flag formation.
  • Lagging momentum indicators, including the Relative Strength Index (RSI) and Stochastic Oscillator, remain constructively aligned with the underlying price action, tracking positively without exhibiting severe divergence.
  • The latest COT report released by the CFTC on Friday, October 16th, 2026, which includes data up to the end of day, Tuesday, October 13th, 2026, reflects that the most recent decline in gold price, which began in August of 2026, was accompanied by relatively unchanged open interest and declining volume. This suggests that the COT data did not support the price drop and a potential change in sentiment.

Conclusion

In summary, the outlook for XAU/USD remains framed by a tug-of-war between persistent hawkish central bank expectations and a constructively bullish long-term technical structure. While sustained inflationary pressure and market expectations of “higher for longer” Federal Reserve interest rates present ongoing macroeconomic headwinds—dampening bullion demand via elevated real yields and a strong U.S. dollar—the technical picture suggests that the recent price consolidation forms a bullish flag within a broader secular uptrend. A decisive breakout above immediate technical resistance around the 4,260–4,408 confluence region would signal a resumption of the broader rally, whereas a breakdown below primary support at 4,000–4,120 could expose lower pivot levels near 3,829.

data.title: Alphabet (GOOGL) Q3 earnings preview: US$200 billion AI capex test puts major uptrend at risk
data.description:
Referenced assets

Key takeaways

  • Google Cloud is the key growth catalyst, but investors will watch whether rapid AI-driven revenue expansion is matched by healthy margins and cash generation.
  • Capex and free cash flow are the biggest valuation risks, especially if Alphabet raises spending again without clearer evidence of improving AI returns.
  • Technically, 359.44 is the key resistance, while a break below 300.44 may expose 270.70 and signal a deeper deterioration in the major uptrend.

Ahead of Wednesday’s Q3 2026 earnings, Alphabet (GOOGL) faces a critical test of whether surging demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing can sustain its rapid Google Cloud growth while offsetting mounting concerns over infrastructure spending, free cash flow and profitability.

Alphabet is expected to release its Q3 results after the US market closes on Wednesday, 28 October 2026, with its earnings conference call scheduled for 4:30 pm Eastern Time.

Based on the street’s expectations, there is an underlying divergence: revenue is expected to increase by nearly 25% year-on-year to US$127.92B, but EPS growth is projected at just 5.6% year-on-year to US$3.02.

Highlighting the market’s focus on whether AI infrastructure costs are beginning to dilute underlying earnings growth. EPS comparisons also require care because Alphabet’s Q2 results included unusually large investment-related gains.

Following weakness in AI-linked technology stocks since the start of October, investors are increasingly questioning whether aggressive capital expenditure commitments will generate sufficient returns to justify elevated valuations.

Alphabet’s shares recorded a loss of 6.34% from the start of October through 26 October 2026, reflecting broader weakness in AI-related technology stocks, with juggernaut Nvidia and the US PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index declining by 6.44% and 13.61% respectively (see Fig. 1).

Ahead of Alphabet’s Q3 earnings release, options markets are pricing an approximately ±6.0% move in Alphabet’s (GOOGL) shares as of 26 October 2026, almost on par with its 10-year average peak earnings-day movement of 6.6%, according to data from EarningsWatcher.

Against this backdrop, Alphabet’s earnings reaction is likely to hinge on six key fundamentals.

1. Google Cloud: the most important earnings growth catalyst

Google Cloud revenue surged 82% year on year to US$24.8 billion in Q2 2026, driven by enterprise AI infrastructure, enterprise AI solutions and core cloud services. Cloud growth significantly outpaced the wider group’s 24% revenue expansion. [1]

Importantly, Cloud has become Alphabet’s clearest avenue for monetising the AI infrastructure boom, benefiting from rising demand for Google Cloud Platform, Gemini-related workloads and its proprietary Tensor Processing Units (TPUs).

J.P. Morgan recently raised its Alphabet price target from US$420 to US$425, expecting Google Cloud’s Q3 revenue to approximately double from the same period a year ago.

2. Google Search advertising: can AI strengthen rather than undermine its core business?

Google Search remains Alphabet’s largest profit engine and an important source of funding for its capital-intensive AI expansion.

In Q2, Google Services revenue increased 15% year on year to US$94.5 billion, supported by 17% growth in Google Search and other advertising revenue, while YouTube advertising revenue increased 13%.

Traders will likely focus on whether AI-powered Search experiences, including AI Overviews and Gemini integration, are driving higher engagement and commercial search activity without undermining traditional advertising monetisation.

The market is particularly sensitive to whether conversational AI services divert users from conventional search queries and reduce the number of profitable advertising opportunities.

3. Capital expenditure and free cash flow: the biggest valuation risk

Alphabet raised its full-year 2026 capital expenditure guidance by US$15 billion to US$195 billion–US$205 billion following its Q2 earnings, reflecting accelerated investment in AI computing, data centres and network infrastructure.

The spending increase comes amid mounting concerns over the sustainability of the AI investment cycle. In the first six months of 2026 alone, Alphabet recorded US$80.6 billion in capital expenditure, compared with US$39.6 billion during the same period in 2025. [2]

Of particular concern, Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of approximately US$5.9 billion in Q2 despite strong revenue growth.

Traders will focus on three questions: whether 2026 spending guidance will increase again, whether management expects another substantial rise in 2027, and whether AI-generated revenue can eventually outpace growth in infrastructure costs.

4. Operating margins: Is AI growth translating into higher profitability?

Alphabet’s Q2 operating income rose 30% year on year, with its operating margin expanding by two percentage points to 34%.

However, rising depreciation, energy requirements, personnel expenses, and infrastructure costs could gradually erode operating leverage as new data-centre capacity comes online.

Investors will closely monitor Google Cloud operating profitability alongside Alphabet’s consolidated operating margin to determine whether the rapid expansion in AI-related revenue is translating into sustainable earnings growth.

A further complication is Alphabet’s investment-related gains. Q2 reported EPS of US$9.11 was significantly boosted by non-operating investment gains, while underlying EPS excluding those gains was approximately US$2.85.

5. Gemini, TPUs and enterprise AI monetisation

Beyond the headline Cloud revenue numbers, investors will assess whether Alphabet’s vertically integrated AI strategy is generating a sustainable competitive advantage.

Alphabet’s proprietary TPU infrastructure provides an alternative to Nvidia GPUs, while Gemini models and enterprise AI services offer additional monetisation opportunities across Google Cloud, Workspace and consumer products.

In Q2, Alphabet began recognising revenue from direct TPU sales, while its Cloud order backlog reportedly reached US$514 billion.

This creates an important potential growth driver; Alphabet can benefit not only from operating its own AI infrastructure but also from supplying computing capacity and specialised hardware to external customers.

6. Forward guidance and macroeconomic conditions

Alphabet reports during a period of elevated uncertainty surrounding US interest rates, inflation and the sustainability of AI infrastructure investment.

The recent weakness in technology and semiconductor stocks has been amplified by concerns over higher Treasury yields and the potential for additional Federal Reserve tightening.

This environment creates two distinct risks for Alphabet.

First, higher interest rates increase the discount rate applied to future earnings, potentially weighing on valuation multiples even if its operational performance remains strong.

Second, persistent inflation and higher energy prices could raise data-centre operating costs while dampening corporate advertising budgets and enterprise technology spending.

At the same time, a resilient US economy and sustained enterprise investment in AI could provide an offsetting tailwind for both Google Search advertising and Google Cloud.

Share-price implication: Strong fourth-quarter guidance, continued advertising resilience, and confident AI spending commentary could support a recovery in Alphabet’s shares. Conversely, weaker advertising demand, accelerating infrastructure costs, or more cautious management commentary could reinforce recent selling pressure across AI-related technology stocks.

Fundamental bottom line: what matters most for traders

Alphabet’s Q3 earnings reaction will likely hinge on four key factors: Google Cloud growth, Search advertising resilience, AI capital expenditure and operating margin performance, with forward guidance playing a decisive role in determining the stock’s post-earnings direction.

The bull case is clean earnings beat, accelerating Google Cloud revenue growth, resilient Search advertising demand and improving AI monetisation, supported by stable capital expenditure guidance and healthy operating margins.

This would reinforce Alphabet’s competitive advantage in AI infrastructure and potentially trigger further valuation expansion.

The bear case is not necessarily disappointing headline earnings, but signs that AI infrastructure spending is rising faster than revenue and profitability.

Slowing Cloud growth, weaker Search monetisation, margin compression or another substantial increase in 2027 capital expenditure expectations may trigger selling pressure, particularly amid heightened scrutiny of AI investment returns.

Let’s now focus on the medium-term outlook of Alphabet’s share price from a technical analysis perspective.

Technical analysis: Major uptrend in jeopardy

Since printing its current all-time intraday high of 408.61 on 18 May 2026, Alphabet (GOOGL) has staged a corrective decline of 22.9%, hitting a low of 314.90 on 23 July 2026.

Recent price action in GOOGL suggests that the bears are likely in control, and it faces an increasing risk of a breakdown from its current major uptrend phase, in place since the 7 April 2025 low of 140.53 (see Fig. 2).

GOOGL has staged a bearish breakdown below its 50- and 200-day moving averages.

In addition, the volatility-adjusted relative strength (VARS) of GOOGL against the Nasdaq 100 exchange-traded fund (QQQ) has trended downward since 16 October 2026, indicating further potential underperformance of GOOGL relative to the Nasdaq 100.

Watch the 359.44 key medium-term pivotal resistance to maintain the bearish bias for GOOGL; a break below 300.44 support (also the lower boundary of the major ascending channel) may trigger another potential multi-week corrective down move to expose the next medium-term support at 270.70 in the first step.

On the other hand, a clearance and a daily close above 359.44 would invalidate the bearish bias, with the next medium-term resistance at 383.00, before a potential retest of the current all-time intraday high of 408.61.

data.title: The US labour market is losing momentum – as is the USD
data.description:
Referenced assets

  • The U.S. labor market is losing momentum, but not collapsing. Nonfarm payrolls rose by only 57,000, previous months were revised lower, and hiring has clearly slowed, while layoffs remain limited.
  • The drop in unemployment is less positive than it looks. The unemployment rate fell to 4.2%, but this was partly due to a decline in labor force participation to 61.5%, meaning some people stopped actively looking for work.
  • The report reduced pressure on the Fed to tighten policy further. Slower job growth and easing wage pressure revived hopes for future rate cuts, weakened the dollar, and supported assets such as gold, Bitcoin, and EUR/USD.

June data from the U.S. labor market showed a clear weakening in employment momentum. Nonfarm payrolls increased by only 57,000, significantly below economists’ expectations. In addition, data for the previous two months were revised downward, weakening earlier signals that had suggested greater resilience in the labor market.

At first glance, the decline in the unemployment rate to 4.2% appeared positive. However, this is not an unambiguous sign of improvement. The drop in unemployment was accompanied by a marked decline in labor force participation. The participation rate fell to 61.5%, reaching its lowest level in more than five years. This means that some individuals stopped actively looking for work and were therefore no longer included in unemployment statistics.

Companies are not conducting mass layoffs, but they are hiring more cautiously

The report does not point to a labor market collapse, but it does show increasing caution among employers. Initial jobless claims remained almost unchanged, suggesting that the scale of layoffs remains limited. The issue, therefore, is not a sharp reduction in employment, but a weaker willingness among companies to create new jobs.

The largest decline in employment was recorded in the leisure and hospitality sector. This is particularly important because, at this time of year, the industry typically increases seasonal hiring. Weaker-than-usual employment growth may indicate a more cautious approach by companies toward consumer demand and future operating costs.

At the same time, some sectors continued to support the labor market. Healthcare and social assistance remained the main source of employment growth. Job numbers also increased in manufacturing and construction. Weakness persisted, however, in the information sector, where employment declined for the seventeenth time in the past eighteen months.

Wages are rising, but inflationary pressure is easing

Average hourly earnings rose by 3.5% year over year in June. This increase shows that wages are still growing, but they are no longer generating inflationary pressure as strong as during the period of peak labor market tightness. For the Federal Reserve, this may be an argument that employment conditions remain relatively stable and do not require an abrupt policy response.

From the perspective of households, however, the picture is less favorable. Slower employment growth means fewer opportunities to find a new job, while inflation continues to limit the real purchasing power of wages. Even if nominal wages are rising, many workers may not feel a clear improvement in their financial situation.

Markets took note of the report’s weakness

The release triggered a moderately positive reaction in financial markets. The S&P 500 opened higher, while U.S. Treasury yields declined. Investors scaled back expectations for further interest rate hikes by the Fed, although they still priced in at least one rate increase this year.

The market reaction shows that weaker employment data were interpreted as a factor reducing pressure on the central bank. If the labor market continues to lose momentum, the Fed may have fewer reasons to tighten monetary policy further.

A mixed picture of the U.S. economy

The data were disappointing, but they should not fundamentally change the overall assessment of the economy. The labor market reflects uneven economic growth, in which some sectors are still creating jobs while others are clearly slowing. From the Fed’s perspective, the situation does not look alarming, as the labor market is not generating additional inflationary pressure. For American households, however, it means more difficult conditions, especially when limited employment opportunities coincide with persistently high living costs.

Kevin Warsh’s first press conference as FOMC Chair was perceived as hawkish and fueled concerns about an interest rate hike in the United States. As a result, the dollar strengthened significantly in recent weeks. Following today’s NFP report, hopes for an interest rate cut have resurfaced. Of course, with core PCE inflation currently at 3.4% year over year, this remains unlikely. Nevertheless, today’s reading creates a balance between arguments for monetary easing and monetary tightening, given the Fed’s dual mandate of maximum employment and price stability. It was precisely these hopes that led to a weakening of the dollar. EUR/USD is currently trading at 1.1446, up 0.59%. Instruments quoted in USD, which have recently failed to generate returns for investors, also deserve attention. Gold is up 2.37% today, while Bitcoin has gained 2.64%.

A labor market without collapse, but also without strength

The June report shows that the U.S. labor market is in a phase of clear slowdown. There are no signs of mass layoffs or a sharp deterioration in conditions, but it is becoming increasingly difficult to describe the market as strong. Companies are acting cautiously, new jobs are being created more slowly, and the decline in unemployment is partly the result of lower labor force participation.

The key takeaway from the report is therefore that the labor market is not collapsing, but it is losing resilience. For the Fed, this means less pressure from wages and employment, while for workers it means more challenging job-search conditions and limited improvement in real incomes.

data.title: Bitcoin Deepens Losses - Crypto Market Under Pressure
data.description:
Referenced assets

  • Bitcoin is under strong selling pressure, falling over 17% in a week and dropping below USD 60,000. The decline was intensified by USD 532 million in long liquidations on Binance, which triggered additional forced selling.
  • Market sentiment worsened after Strategy sold part of its bitcoin holdings. Although the sale was small — 32 BTC for USD 2.5 million — it raised concerns that the largest corporate bitcoin holder could make further sales in the future.
  • The broader crypto market is weak due to macro and demand concerns. Strong U.S. labor data reduced hopes for rate cuts, retail investors are shifting toward AI-related tech stocks, ETF inflows remain too small to support prices, and security concerns after the Zcash vulnerability further damaged trust.

Bitcoin has come under heavy selling pressure and has already lost more than 17 percent since the beginning of the week. On Friday, its price fell below the psychological barrier of USD 60,000, increasing investor concerns about a further deepening of the correction. Bitcoin has fallen below its 200-week SMA for the first time in three years. From its all-time high near USD 126,000, the leading cryptocurrency has already lost more than half of its value.

Long liquidations increase pressure on the market

The scale of the declines was amplified by the forced closure of leveraged positions. Over the past 24 hours, long positions worth USD 532 million were liquidated on the Binance exchange. Such a large wave of liquidations shows that many investors betting on a bitcoin rebound were forced to close their positions, which further increased selling pressure in the market.

This mechanism often deepens declines, as automatic liquidations lead to further sell orders. As a result, the market can move more sharply than would be implied solely by incoming macroeconomic data or the decisions of the largest investors.

Strategy’s Bitcoin sale weighed on sentiment

One of the factors worsening sentiment was the news that Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin and a company associated with Michael Saylor, had sold part of its bitcoin holdings. The company sold 32 bitcoins for USD 2.5 million. Although the transaction was small compared with the company’s overall portfolio, it carried significant symbolic weight.

It was only Strategy’s second bitcoin sale since it began making purchases in 2020. The company explained the decision as necessary to pay coupons to holders of preferred shares, but investors interpreted it as a possible weakening of the long-standing narrative of holding bitcoin indefinitely.

The market is primarily concerned that this small sale could foreshadow further, larger transactions in the future. This risk was highlighted by Peter Schiff, a well-known bitcoin critic, who stressed that the problem is not the scale of the current sale itself, but its potential consequences for investor confidence. Before this transaction, Strategy had reportedly purchased a total of 843,738 BTC for nearly USD 64 billion, which is why any change in the company’s strategy is being closely watched by the market.

Declines spread across the entire cryptocurrency market

Selling pressure was not limited to bitcoin. Ethereum fell by around 23 percent over the week to USD 1,555, while Solana lost about 22 percent, dropping to USD 63.75. Weakness was also visible in shares of companies linked to cryptocurrencies. Strategy’s stock fell by almost 10 percent, while Coinbase shares declined by 8.4 percent.

A modest positive signal came from inflows into U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs yesterday after 13 days of outflows. However, the scale of these inflows, amounting to just over USD 3 million, was too small to change the overall market picture. In practice, this means that institutional demand remains too weak to effectively stop the current sell-off.

Strong U.S. Data reduces hopes for rate cuts

Sentiment was also hurt by strong data from the U.S. labor market. Nonfarm payrolls rose by 172,000 in May, clearly above expectations. Such data reduces the likelihood of swift interest rate cuts in the United States, which is unfavorable for risk assets, including cryptocurrencies.

The strong labor market report weakened the narrative of imminent monetary policy easing, while bitcoin currently lacks a clear macroeconomic catalyst that could support a rebound.

Retail investors shift their attention to tech stocks

An additional problem for the crypto market is the outflow of some retail investors toward technology stocks, especially companies linked to artificial intelligence. Retail investors have largely left the cryptocurrency market and returned to equities, making it difficult to identify new sources of demand for bitcoin.

In an environment of weakening interest and a lack of fresh capital, every negative piece of news can trigger a stronger price reaction. This applies both to macroeconomic data and to decisions by major entities holding significant bitcoin reserves.

Security issues weaken trust in Crypto

The cryptocurrency market is also struggling with concerns over trust in the security of blockchain technology. Investors paid particular attention to a vulnerability in the Zcash network, after which the cryptocurrency’s price fell by more than 40 percent in a single day. Developers fixed the bug, but they were unable to clearly determine whether it had been exploited to create additional tokens.

This situation increased concerns that increasingly advanced artificial intelligence models may in the future help detect similar vulnerabilities in other cryptocurrency projects. For a market already under downward pressure, such information further worsens sentiment.

Lack of new sources of demand makes a rebound difficult

The current sell-off in bitcoin is the result of several negative factors overlapping: strong U.S. economic data, reduced expectations for interest rate cuts, investors shifting toward technology stocks, concerns about Strategy’s future actions, trust issues related to the security of some crypto projects, and the large scale of long liquidations in the leveraged instruments market.

Bitcoin remains under pressure, and the lack of clear new sources of demand means that a quick and sustained rebound may be difficult. The market appears weakened, and investors are watching increasingly closely to see whether the drop below USD 60,000 proves to be only a brief breach of an important level or a continuation of the downward trend that began in October 2025.

data.title: Chart alert: Bitcoin (BTC/USD) potential near-term bullish reversal emerging from the sub-$70K plunge
data.description:
Referenced assets

Key takeaways

  • Bitcoin plunged 16% over the past two weeks and briefly fell below the US$70,000 psychological level after MicroStrategy’s partial Bitcoin sale shattered the long-standing “never sell” narrative that had supported market sentiment.
  • Despite the sharp decline, several contrarian indicators suggest selling pressure may be nearing exhaustion, including an extremely oversold daily RSI reading, a surge in long-position liquidations, and signs of renewed accumulation by long-term holders.
  • Technical and on-chain metrics indicate the potential for a near-term bullish reversal above the key US$62,250 support level, with upside targets at US$74,880 and US$82,815 if buying momentum returns.

Let’s unpack the primary drivers and the technical setup.

The plunge and its fundamental catalysts

On Monday and Tuesday (1–2 June 2026), the cryptocurrency market absorbed a significant psychological blow. Spot BTC/USD tumbled sharply, slipping below the $70,000 psychological threshold and falling 16% over the past two weeks. It printed an intraday low of $65,370 on Wednesday, 3 June 2026.

The dominant driver of this week’s movement was the revelation that MicroStrategy, the world’s largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, sold a portion of its holdings for the first time in four years.

While the market impact is less about the absolute volume of the sale and more about the erosion of consensus, it effectively shattered founder Michael Saylor’s widely echoed “never sell” iron law.

This pivot disrupted the pricing anchor the market had historically relied on, injecting uncertainty and triggering a wave of defensive selling.

Technical and on-chain analysis suggesting a setup for a bullish reversal

The 16% plunge in BTC/USD has left it hovering just above its $62,250 key medium-term pivotal support and the lower boundary of its long-term secular ascending channel running from the December 2018 low.

In addition, the daily RSI momentum indicator hit a significant oversold level of 21.8 on Tuesday, 2 June 2026, its lowest since 5 February 2026, triggering a 35% rally in BTC/USD over the next three months.

Secondly, utilising TradingView’s crypto derivatives indicators for crypto futures and perpetual swaps, such as from Bybit, Binance, and OKX.

Aggregated long liquidation data (derived from various exchanges) spiked to $482 million on Tuesday, 2 June 2026, indicating that many leveraged long positions in Bitcoin futures and perpetual swaps were forced closed due to margin calls.

A similar rise in long liquidations ($481 million) also occurred on 5 February 2026, when capitulation led to a 35% rally in BTC/USD.

Thirdly, on-chain indicator: the percentage of 1-year active supply for Bitcoin has declined steadily over the past three weeks, from 40.3% on 23 April 2026 to 39.3% on Wednesday, 3 June 2026, at the time of writing.

Active supply 1-year measures the total number of unique cryptocurrency units that have moved at least once over the past 1 year. This metric tracks the portion of supply that has been involved in on-chain transactions during the trailing 365-day period.

A decreasing active supply often signals accumulation by long-term holders, a bullish condition for Bitcoin in the current context.

Hence, based on these factors, BTC/USD is now ripe for a potential near-term bullish reversal above the $62,250 key medium-term support, with intermediate resistance at $74,880. A clearance above it would signal a retest of the $82,815 medium-term resistance (also close to the 200-day moving average).

On the other hand, a daily close below $62,250 invalidates the recovery scenario and extends the corrective decline towards the $57,590/52,590 long-term pivotal support zone.
